guideTitle: Best RV Air Conditioners for Travel Trailers (2026)
metaTitle: Best RV Air Conditioners for Travel Trailers
metaDescription: Six rooftop air conditioners for travel trailers compared on drop-in compatibility, R32 refrigerant, low profile options and electrical demands.
expertTake: The Dometic FreshJet 3 R32 is the travel trailer pick because it is backward compatible with existing Dometic and competitor air returns and controls, which makes it the easiest true swap. The MrCool TravelCool is the unusual choice for an owner who wants an 11 inch ductless profile. Skip the biggest 18,000 BTU units unless your trailer has a lot of glass and a 50 amp inlet.
introParagraphs: The travel trailer is the home turf of the rooftop air conditioner. Most came from the factory with one unit, a ceiling assembly that matches it and a power system sized around a single compressor, which makes a like-for-like swap the most common repair on the lot.

That makes compatibility the first filter. A unit that reuses your existing return and controls saves a half day of ceiling work, while one that wants new interior parts changes the economics of the whole job. We rank the field by how easily each fits a typical trailer, then by capacity, noise and electrical demand.

products.name: Dometic FreshJet 3 Series R32 rooftop RV air conditioner

specList.label: Compatibility
specList.value: Existing Dometic and competitor returns and controls

products.description:
Compatibility is the headline feature of this FreshJet 3: the maker says it works with existing Dometic and competitor air returns and controls, which means the ceiling assembly and thermostat you already own can usually stay. In a travel trailer that cuts the job to the roof and the wiring, which is why this is the easiest honest swap on the market.

It uses R32 refrigerant, which the maker says carries a lower environmental impact and better energy efficiency, and the body is 14 percent lighter than the older Brisk II. That helps when two people are lifting it onto a trailer roof. No BTU figure appears in the listing, so check the model code against your trailer before ordering.

It is a fixed-speed machine, so a soft start helps on a small generator. Compared with the TOSOT it is less quiet by claim but far easier to fit. Give the filter a monthly wash and check the gasket each spring.
products.bestFor: Travel trailers replacing an existing unit with the least interior work.
pros: Reuses existing Dometic and competitor returns and controls
14 percent lighter than the Brisk II
cons: BTU rating is not stated in the listing

products.name: MrCool TravelCool RV heat and AC system, ductless 15K, black
products.description:
MrCool is better known for ductless mini splits, and the TravelCool brings that background to a rooftop package with a quoted 11 inch low profile. At 15,000 BTU it is a heat and AC system rather than a plain cooler, and the maker says it cools in outdoor temperatures up to 109 degrees Fahrenheit.

That low profile helps with clearance and wind drag on a trailer that travels often. It is a ductless design, so it suits a center ceiling assembly, and the heat function gives mild-weather warmth. The listing is short on detail, so confirm interior compatibility, voltage needs and control options before buying.

Next to the Dometic it offers a thinner shroud and a heat function at the cost of drop-in simplicity. Keep the filter clean, inspect the roof seal each spring and check the shroud screws after the first trip.
products.bestFor: Travel trailers that want a slim roof profile and built-in heat.
pros: 11 inch low profile reduces height and drag
Quoted cooling up to 109 F outdoor
cons: Listing is thin on interior compatibility details
Less brand support than the traditional marques

products.name: TOSOT 16,000 BTU RV AC heat pump, 43 dB claim, white
products.description:
A travel trailer bedroom sits close to the roof unit, and the TOSOT claims 43 dB, which the maker says is 32 percent quieter than a standard RV air conditioner. It pairs that with 16,000 BTU of cooling and a 12,500 BTU heat pump, giving a large trailer both capacity and shoulder-season heat.

That capacity is more than most trailers need, so it suits the 30 foot and longer models with slides and big windows. The heat pump saves furnace runtime in spring and fall but fades near freezing. A fixed-speed compressor of this size is a heavy generator load.

Against the Dometic it trades the drop-in compatibility for quiet and heat. Check the control board against your ceiling panel before ordering, fit a soft start if you use a generator and wash the filter monthly.
products.bestFor: Large trailers where bedroom noise and mild-weather heat matter.
pros: 43 dB claim is the quietest here
cons: Large fixed-speed compressor loads a small generator

products.name: Arsenda 18K BTU RV AC with heat pump, 50 dB, non-ducted
products.description:
Arsenda gives a travel trailer 18,000 BTU of cooling and a heat pump with a quoted 50 dB, which is a lot of capacity for a modest price. It is aimed at buyers who want a heat pump in a non-ducted unit without paying the established-brand premium.

The unit requires both 115V AC and 12V DC power, so a drained house battery stops it even with shore power connected. At 18,000 BTU it is the biggest compressor here, which means a heavy startup surge and a need for a soft start or a strong supply. In a smaller trailer it will cycle.

Against the TOSOT it gives more capacity and a looser noise claim for a lower price. Check the 12V feed, confirm the interior panel fits and wash the filter monthly.
products.bestFor: Large or sunny trailers wanting a heat pump on a budget.
pros: 18,000 BTU with a heat pump included
cons: Biggest startup surge in the guide

products.name: TUSOMA 18,000 BTU RV AC with heat pump, 110-120V non-ducted

specList.label: Targets
specList.value: RVs, campers, travel trailers, fifth wheels

products.description:
TUSOMA positions this 18,000 BTU unit for year-round climate control, combining cooling with a heat pump aimed at four-season camping. It lists travel trailers and fifth wheels among its targets, so the roof opening and fit are meant to be standard.

Like similar large units it needs both 115V AC and 12V DC for correct operation, so the wiring and the house battery are part of the purchase. The compressor is big, so a soft start or a strong pedestal is wise, and in a small trailer the capacity is more than the volume can use.

Compared with the Arsenda it is similar in capacity and design, with less published detail on noise. Verify the interior parts, fit a soft start and inspect the 12V feed every season.
products.bestFor: Large trailers camping through all four seasons.
pros: 18,000 BTU with a heat pump for four seasons
cons: No published noise figure in the data

products.name: Treeligo 18,000 BTU RV AC with heat, 115V non-ducted, 50 dB
products.description:
Treeligo's 115V unit packs 18,000 BTU with heating and a quoted 50 dB, in a housing described as UV-resistant for roof exposure. It aims at all-weather comfort in a non-ducted package that fits a standard travel trailer roof.

The selling point is simplicity: capacity and heat in one unit, at a price below the established marques. The drawbacks are the large startup surge and thinner parts support than Dometic. In a smaller trailer it is oversized.

Compared with the TUSOMA it states the noise figure and the power need more plainly. Plan a soft start, wash the filter monthly and inspect the roof gasket each spring.
products.bestFor: Large trailers wanting capacity and heat at a low price.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The biggest cost in a trailer swap is often the interior. A unit that reuses your existing air return and controls, as the FreshJet 3 R32 claims, saves hours of ceiling work. A unit that needs new interior parts, such as some value brands, changes the real price. Look at your ceiling assembly and thermostat brand before comparing units. Mixing brands can work, but wall thermostats and ceiling boards are often proprietary, and a mismatch leaves you with a unit that runs only in manual mode.

A trailer up to about 25 feet cools well with 13,500 BTU, while 28 to 32 foot trailers with slides and big windows suit 15,000 to 16,000 BTU. The 18,000 BTU units here are for the biggest or sunniest trailers. An oversized unit short-cycles and leaves the air humid, so do not buy the biggest number.

A taller shroud adds wind drag and may catch a low branch. The MrCool TravelCool quotes an 11 inch profile, which helps on a trailer that travels often. Measure your travel height and the obstacles on your usual routes before paying for a slimmer unit. A few inches matters at a fuel canopy or under a campground tree, and costs nothing once the trailer is bought.

R32 refrigerant, used in the Dometic FreshJet 3 R32, carries heat efficiently and needs a smaller charge by weight than older R410A designs. That helps efficiency and environmental impact. Any sealed-system service still needs a certified technician.

Most travel trailers have a 30 amp inlet, which feeds one air conditioner plus modest loads. An 18,000 BTU unit surges hard at startup, so a soft start or a 50 amp inlet is advisable. Units that need both 115V AC and 12V DC, like the Arsenda, also depend on a healthy house battery.

A trailer air conditioner often fails on the hottest weekend. Dometic has wide parts stocking and technician familiarity, while newer brands may mean waiting for a part. Weigh the price saving against the downtime risk, and carry a spare capacitor and filter either way.

howWeEvaluated.title: Swap compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored units that reuse existing returns and controls, led by the Dometic FreshJet 3 R32. We noted where a listing was thin on interior detail. A cheap unit that needs new parts was marked down.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched 15,000 BTU to 18,000 BTU units to trailer size and sun load. Oversized units were flagged for short cycling. The TOSOT's 16,000 BTU scored for large trailers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Profile and weight
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the MrCool's 11 inch profile and the Dometic's 14 percent weight saving. Lighter and lower units earned credit for handling and clearance. Weight claims were treated as guides.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise and heat
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the 43 dB TOSOT and the 50 dB Arsenda and Treeligo, and heat pump against plain heating. Claims were treated as maker figures. Sleeping near the unit raised the weight of noise.

howWeEvaluated.title: Support
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered brand parts stock, technician familiarity and published detail. The Dometic led, and thinly documented units fell behind. Price savings were credited but weighed against downtime.

maintenance.why: A clogged filter freezes the coil and weakens cooling. A quick wash keeps the compressor healthy, and a spare filter in the drawer means a wash day never leaves the unit running bare.
Trailers flex on the road, which cracks sealant. A leak behind the ceiling is costly, and a trailer stored under a cover can hide a slow drip for months until the panel stains.
Vibration loosens hardware and shifts the gasket. Even torque keeps the seal, and a dab of thread-locking compound on the nuts keeps them from backing off on a rough forest road.
Roof dust blocks heat rejection. Use low-pressure water, and wash from the inside of the fins outward so debris leaves the way it came in instead of packing deeper into the coil.
The Arsenda and TUSOMA need 12V DC. A corroded terminal stops them.

faq.q: What size air conditioner does a travel trailer need?
faq.a: Trailers up to about 25 feet cool well with 13,500 BTU, while 28 to 32 foot trailers suit 15,000 to 16,000 BTU. Oversizing causes short cycling and a clammy cabin. The real sizing inputs are sun exposure, slides, windows and insulation, so a shaded 28 foot trailer can need less than a sunlit 25 foot one with a big front window.

faq.q: Can I replace my air conditioner without changing the ceiling?
faq.a: Often yes, if the new unit is backward compatible with your return and controls. Dometic claims this for the FreshJet 3 R32, but confirm your own model. Take a photo of the existing ceiling assembly, note the thermostat brand and measure the roof opening, then compare them with the listing before you order anything, because the interior is where swaps run over budget.

faq.q: Do I need a soft start?
faq.a: On a generator or a weak pedestal, usually. Fixed-speed compressors surge at startup, and a soft start cuts it sharply. It is a small module that wires in near the compressor, and many owners install one in an afternoon, which makes it the cheapest upgrade in the whole category.

faq.q: Is a heat pump worth it?
faq.a: For shoulder-season warmth, yes. It saves furnace fuel, but output fades near freezing. A trailer that camps mostly in summer gets little from it, while one that lives in spring and fall conditions will use it most mornings.

faq.q: Is an 18,000 BTU unit too much?
faq.a: For most trailers, yes. It suits only the largest or sunniest ones, and it needs a strong electrical supply. If the trailer sits in a hot climate with a dark roof, a variable-speed or inverter unit is a better answer than simply stepping up in BTU.

faq.q: How long does a travel trailer air conditioner last?
faq.a: Many run for a decade or more when the filter and coil are kept clean and the sealed system stays healthy. Neglected filters, a dirty condenser and loose mounting hardware are what shorten that life, and none of them cost much to prevent. A unit that starts to hum without cooling usually needs a capacitor or a refrigerant check by a technician.
